questions.question_text: For the function $f(x) = \dfrac{8}{x}$, which statement correctly describes its behaviour as $x \to \infty$ and as $x \to -\infty$?

options.text: As $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from above; as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from below.
As $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from below; as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from above.
options.why: Assumed $k < 0$, reversing the signs of $y$.
Assumed the quotient grows with the denominator instead of approaching zero.
Evaluated the function at $x = 1$ and $x = -1$ instead of describing its behaviour at infinity.

questions.solution_text:
For $f(x) = \dfrac{8}{x}$ with $k = 8 > 0$:
As $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from above.
As $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from below.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes the end behaviour of $f(x) = \dfrac{5}{x}$ as $x \to \infty$ and as $x \to -\infty$?

options.text: As $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from above; as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from below.
As $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from below; as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from above.
options.why: Reversed the signs of $y$ in the first and third quadrants.
Confused the end behaviour with a linear or cubic polynomial function.
Assumed the horizontal limit approaches the numerator $k$ rather than zero.

questions.solution_text:
Since $k = 5 > 0$:
When $x$ is large and positive, $y = \dfrac{5}{x} > 0$ and approaches $0$, so $y \to 0$ from above.
When $x$ is large and negative, $y = \dfrac{5}{x} < 0$ and approaches $0$, so $y \to 0$ from below.

options.why: Ignored the negative sign in the numerator, making the outputs positive for positive $x$.
Confused behaviour as $x \to \infty$ with behaviour as positive $x$ approaches zero.
Evaluated the function at $x = 1$ instead of describing its behaviour as $x \to \infty$.

questions.solution_text:
For positive $x$, $-\dfrac{6}{x} < 0$.
As $x \to \infty$, these negative values approach $0$ from below.

questions.question_text: For $f(x) = \dfrac{7}{x}$ and $g(x) = \dfrac{2}{x}$, which statement correctly describes their behaviour as $x \to -\infty$?

options.why: Treated the outputs as positive despite the negative values of $x$.
Used the numerators as the limiting values instead of dividing by increasingly large negative values.
Assumed the outputs grow in magnitude as the denominator grows in magnitude.

questions.solution_text:
Both numerators are positive, so both functions have negative outputs when $x < 0$.
As $x \to -\infty$, both outputs approach $0$ from below.

questions.question_text: For $y = -\dfrac{15}{x}$, what are its quadrants and end behaviour as $x \to \infty$?

options.why: Ignored the negative reciprocal constant and used the quadrants and end behaviour for a positive constant.
Treated the numerator as the limiting value instead of zero.
Named adjacent quadrants instead of Quadrants $2$ and $4$, and incorrectly made the outputs positive for positive $x$.

questions.solution_text:
Since $k = -15 < 0$, the branches lie in Quadrants $2$ and $4$.
As $x \to \infty$, $y = -\dfrac{15}{x} < 0$, so $y \to 0$ from below.

questions.question_text: In which quadrants does the graph of $f(x) = -\dfrac{9}{x}$ lie?

options.why: Assumed every hyperbola lies in quadrants $1$ and $3$, ignoring the sign of $k$.
Placed both branches on the positive-$x$ side instead of allowing positive and negative inputs.
Placed both branches on the negative-$x$ side instead of allowing positive and negative inputs.

questions.solution_text:
For $f(x) = -\dfrac{9}{x}$, $k = -9 < 0$.
The branches occupy Quadrants $2$ and $4$.

questions.question_text: For $f(x) = -\dfrac{10}{x}$, which statement correctly describes its behaviour as $x \to -\infty$ and as $x \to \infty$?

options.text: As $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from above; as $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from below.
As $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from below; as $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from above.
options.why: Reversed the signs of the outputs: they are positive for negative $x$ and negative for positive $x$.
Assumed the outputs grow like $x$ instead of shrinking in magnitude, and also reversed their signs.

options.text: As $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from above; as $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from above.
options.why: Ignored the negative sign of the outputs for positive $x$.

questions.solution_text:
When $x < 0$, $y = -\dfrac{10}{x} > 0$.
As $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from above.
When $x > 0$, $y < 0$, so as $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from below.

questions.question_text: For $f(x) = -\dfrac{5}{2x}$, which statement correctly gives its quadrants and its behaviour as $x \to -\infty$?

options.why: Ignored the negative sign and used the behaviour for a positive reciprocal constant.
Confused end behaviour at negative infinity with behaviour near zero on the negative side.
Failed to account for the negative denominator when $x < 0$, which makes the quotient positive.

questions.solution_text:
The reciprocal constant is $-\dfrac{5}{2} < 0$, so the branches lie in Quadrants $2$ and $4$.
For negative $x$, $f(x) > 0$; as $x \to -\infty$, $f(x) \to 0$ from above.

questions.question_text: Compare $f(x) = \dfrac{4}{3x}$ and $g(x) = -\dfrac{7}{2x}$. Which statement correctly describes their behaviour as $x \to \infty$ and as $x \to -\infty$?

options.text: As $x \to \infty$, $f(x)$ approaches $0$ from above and $g(x)$ from below; as $x \to -\infty$, $f(x)$ approaches $0$ from below and $g(x)$ from above.
As $x \to \infty$, both approach $0$ from above; as $x \to -\infty$, both approach $0$ from below.
options.why: Ignored the negative numerator of $g(x)$ and gave it the same signs as $f(x)$.

options.text: As $x \to \infty$, $f(x)$ approaches $0$ from below and $g(x)$ from above; as $x \to -\infty$, $f(x)$ approaches $0$ from above and $g(x)$ from below.
options.why: Reversed the output signs for both functions on both sides.

options.text: At both ends, $f(x)$ approaches $\dfrac{4}{3}$ and $g(x)$ approaches $-\dfrac{7}{2}$.
options.why: Used the reciprocal constants as limiting values instead of accounting for division by $x$.

questions.solution_text:
The reciprocal constant of $f(x)$ is positive, so its outputs approach $0$ from above at positive infinity and from below at negative infinity.
The reciprocal constant of $g(x)$ is negative, so its outputs approach $0$ from below at positive infinity and from above at negative infinity.
